In October 2020, a friend asked me a question -

“Do you think there will be a time when we as a society will look back and be horrified at the way our young ones were treated?”

It made me think, and I wrote a post setting out twenty things about the treatment of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities which I thought future generations might one day look back upon and say  “History judged that severely.”  Six years later, I have gone back and read what I wrote. I wish I could say that we had moved forward. I cannot.

In some respects, the problems I wrote about remain exactly as they were. In others, I fear things have become worse. We are now facing major reform of the SEND system in England, with real concern about what future legal protections will look like. In Wales, the Additional Learning Needs system has come into force, yet young people caught in the transition between the old and new systems have themselves had to fight to establish their rights.

More generally, families still contact us every day because they cannot obtain assessments, therapy, suitable education, mental health support or social care without a battle. For those who did not see what I wrote back in 2020, these were the twenty issues I identified.

1. When local authorities relied predominantly upon their own commissioned or employed professionals to assess a child’s special educational needs, while dismissing independent evidence on the basis that it was merely “private”.

2. When the NHS so rarely recommended direct speech and language therapy or occupational therapy, despite the extent of a child’s needs and the importance of that provision to their development.

3. When children and young people’s mental health services discharged even highly vulnerable children, sometimes seemingly driven more by waiting-list pressures and targets than by clinical need.

4. When Tribunals were reluctant to make costs orders against local authorities, even where authorities had behaved unreasonably or failed to comply with basic procedural obligations.

5. When a child with complex needs spanning several different areas could nevertheless be restricted to only two or three professional witnesses in a Tribunal appeal expected to determine all of those needs. 

6. When health and social care provision identified within an EHCP could not be enforced through the SEND Tribunal in the same way as special educational provision, leaving important parts of a child’s support without an effective remedy in that jurisdiction.

7. When allegations of bullying involving disabled or vulnerable children were too often denied or minimised rather than properly investigated and addressed.

8. When parents were frightened to challenge failures in their child’s education or care because they feared being portrayed as difficult, unreasonable or even accused of fabricating their child’s difficulties.

9. When Pathological Demand Avoidance remained controversial and inconsistently recognised, and when sensory integration therapy was frequently dismissed despite families reporting significant sensory difficulties affecting everyday life.

10. When parents were denied legal aid for representation at final SEND Tribunal hearings, while public authorities could spend public money instructing lawyers to defend the decisions being challenged.

11, When extremely anxious children, including those experiencing school-related distress, were still expected to attend mainstream school despite compelling evidence that the environment had become psychologically intolerable for them.

12. When children could struggle to access mental health treatment because their difficulties were attributed to autism or intellectual disability rather than treated as mental health needs requiring proper intervention. 

13. When, in Wales, decisions about whether some of the most complex young people could attend specialist further education could ultimately depend upon government funding decisions, with limited routes of effective challenge.

14. When decisions about provision for children with the greatest needs were made by the very public bodies responsible for paying for that provision, creating an obvious tension between assessed need and financial responsibility.

15. When children were too often judged principally by academic attainment, with insufficient recognition of their practical abilities, independence, creativity, communication, social development and other talents.

16. When parents could be prosecuted because their child was not attending school, even where the child was experiencing profound anxiety or other unmet needs and the parents themselves were desperately seeking help. 

17. When schools could find themselves under pressure to support the position of a local authority, rather than speaking openly and independently about what they believed a child actually required.

18. When disabled students at university could encounter poor understanding of disability, inadequate reasonable adjustments and processes which failed to appreciate how disability affected their ability to study, participate or defend themselves within disciplinary procedures. 

19. When the university complaints system offered students limited practical redress, despite concerns about its independence and despite compensation often being modest even where significant injustice had occurred. 

20. When the heightened risk of suicide and serious mental-health difficulties among autistic people, including those with co-occurring ADHD, received nowhere near the level of public attention, research or urgency that the issue demanded.

Reading that list again in 2026 is sobering. Some of it could have been written yesterday. What troubles me  is that in 2020 I still believed we were moving, however slowly and imperfectly, in the right direction. I ended that post by saying that perhaps all we could do was live with the experiences of the day whilst moving forward, in the hope that one day we might understand them backwards. I regret to say that I no longer feel quite so optimistic.

I fear that we are no longer simply struggling to improve an imperfect system. In some important respects, we may actually be dismantling protections which families fought for over many years. 
So perhaps the question today is far more sobering. It is whether, when people look back at 2026, they will ask why, having known all of this, we allowed ourselves to move backwards.

When Leadership Becomes Ownership
Why Movements Must Build Power that Outlasts Their Leaders

"It would be a profound contradiction if a movement built on self-determination recreated structures in which a small number of organizations or leaders became the arbiters of whose voices counted."

(ADA Watch/CDRJ) The broader civil and human rights ecosystem is caught in an exhausting cycle of top-down leadership. Across our political, cultural, and institutional life, we are witnessing a resurgence of what might be called the heroic—or proprietary—leadership model: leadership organized around centralized authority, institutional gatekeeping, personal branding, and the assumption that legitimacy flows from the top down.

The problem is not strong leadership. Movements need people willing to take responsibility, make difficult decisions, organize resources, articulate vision, and act when circumstances demand action.

The problem begins when leadership becomes an exercise in ownership.

Under the proprietary model, authority is treated as something possessed rather than something exercised in relationship with others. Institutions become territorial. Access becomes conditional. Information becomes currency. Legitimacy is conferred by invitation to the right tables rather than demonstrated through contribution, accountability, and results. In that environment, independent action itself can become threatening.

When authority becomes proprietary, disagreement can easily be recast as disloyalty. That is where gatekeeping can slide into bullying: ridicule, exclusion, intimidation, public diminishment, private pressure, or the use of institutional standing to punish people who refuse to defer. The point is not that every conflict is bullying, or that strong disagreement is inherently abusive. Movements need argument. But when power is used not to answer an argument but to make the person raising it smaller, quieter, or less able to participate, something more serious is happening.

When people or organizations work outside established structures and succeed, the response is sometimes not curiosity about what worked, but suspicion about who gave them permission to do it. Work that bypasses traditional channels may be dismissed as "performative," insufficiently collaborative, or somehow illegitimate because it did not originate within the recognized source of authority.

But movements cannot afford to confuse institutional recognition with movement legitimacy. The real question should be much simpler:

Did the work strengthen the ability of people to act, participate, organize, and exercise power on their own behalf?

That question becomes especially urgent when resources are scarce. Every movement organization operates within limits of money, time, attention, and human capacity. When too much of those resources is consumed defending institutional territory, maintaining unnecessarily heavy structures, resolving status disputes, or navigating internal power struggles, those resources become unavailable for organizing, advocacy, community support, policy work, and leadership development.

Gatekeeping is not only unfair. It is expensive.

Bullying is especially costly in movements because it does not merely wound individuals; it teaches everyone watching what happens to people who challenge concentrated power. That makes bullying more than an interpersonal problem. It becomes a structural one.

Institutions naturally develop incentives to preserve themselves. Leadership positions accumulate authority. Networks become professionalized. Invitations become markers of legitimacy. Over time, structures originally created to serve a movement can begin expecting the movement to serve the structures.

Legacy matters. Institutions preserve memory, expertise, relationships, and hard-won knowledge. But legacy should be a resource for future generations, not a claim of ownership over them.

Civil and human rights movements have confronted this tension before. Ella Baker was among the clearest critics of leadership models built around charismatic authority and dependency. Reflecting on the danger of celebrity leadership, she warned:

"There is also the danger in our culture that because a person is called upon to give public statements and is acclaimed by the establishment, such a person gets to the point of believing that he is the movement."

Her famous observation that "strong people don't need strong leaders" has sometimes been misunderstood as an argument against leadership itself. It was nothing of the kind.

Baker believed deeply in leadership development. Her challenge was to the idea that movements should depend upon singular figures whose authority eclipses the people supposedly being organized. Leadership, in her conception, should multiply human capacity rather than concentrate dependency.

The question is not whether movements need strong leaders. It is whether strong leadership creates more leaders—or more followers.

That distinction matters enormously in the disability rights and justice movement. Our movement grew because people refused to accept decisions made about them without them. People with disabilities challenged institutions that claimed the authority to determine where they should live, whether they could work, whether they belonged in schools and communities, and what kinds of lives they were permitted to imagine.

It would be a profound contradiction if a movement built on self-determination recreated structures in which a small number of organizations or leaders became the arbiters of whose voices counted. And we should be willing to examine who has historically been able to gain access to those positions of authority.

Civil and human rights institutions—including disability organizations—have not existed outside the racial, gender, economic, and professional hierarchies of the larger society. Leadership tables have not always reflected the communities most affected by the decisions being made. People of color, women, LGBTQ+ people, people with significant disabilities, psychiatric survivors, people living in poverty, and others pushed to the margins have too often had to fight not simply for their rights in society, but for full participation within movements created to advance those rights.

Acknowledging that history does not require reducing every leadership failure to identity, nor pretending that representation alone solves questions of power.

I write this as an older white man who has spent much of my adult life in civil and human rights work. That does not disqualify me from leadership, but neither should age, longevity, institutional history, or identity entitle me to authority over those who come next.

If anything, longevity creates a different responsibility: to help build structures through which other people can exercise power without needing our permission.

I name my own position because the pattern I want to describe is not one I see only from the outside. Leaders who have spent decades doing this work, myself included, can become attached to being needed.

Coalition work taught me that responsibility early. Throughout the years, ADA Watch and the National Coalition for Disability Rights (as it was originally named), working with our civil rights, human rights and social justice allies, mobilized opposition to a number of extremist judicial nominations. Our most visible campaign was Jeffrey Sutton's nomination to the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals. Sutton had argued before the Supreme Court in Garrett that state employees could not sue for damages under the Americans with Disabilities Act. When we placed an ad in Roll Call, the point was not to name a "leading" organization. It was to list and elevate hundreds of disability and civil rights organizations, each standing in its own name.

That is what servant architecture looks like in practice. It was a tangible demonstration that no single organization, constituency, or leader can credibly claim to embody the whole. A coalition is strongest not when everyone speaks with one voice, but when people with different histories, identities, constituencies, and perspectives retain their own voices while developing enough shared purpose to act together.

That principle points toward an alternative to proprietary, top-down leadership. The alternative is not leaderlessness, endless consensus, or the romantic assumption that decentralized networks somehow govern themselves.

Distributed leadership requires structure.

It requires transparent rules, accessible information, multiple centers of initiative, accountable decision-making, open pathways for participation, and systems that allow people to contribute without first securing the approval of a centralized authority. Authority becomes something dynamic rather than proprietary. Expertise can exist in many places. Leadership can shift according to the work at hand. Organizations can provide infrastructure without demanding ownership of the movement that infrastructure serves.

This is the distinction between institutional vanity and servant architecture. Institutional vanity asks how to remain indispensable, measuring success through prominence and the concentration of legitimacy. Servant architecture asks how to make participation possible, measuring success by how effectively it distributes tools, information, relationships, and opportunities for action.

This transition is not easy. Institutions rarely surrender centrality voluntarily. But movement leadership should ultimately make itself less indispensable.

The strongest leader is not the person standing permanently at the center of every photograph, table, campaign, or decision. The strongest leader helps create conditions in which people who were once excluded can organize, decide, lead, challenge, build, and eventually reshape the structures themselves. That is not weakness. It is durability.

Movements do not survive because a handful of exceptional people remain permanently in command. They survive because knowledge is shared, relationships extend beyond individuals, leadership reproduces itself, institutions remain porous enough to change, and new people can enter without swearing allegiance to whoever arrived first. The task before us is therefore larger than replacing one generation of leaders with another. It is to change the architecture of leadership itself.

We must move from authority as possession to authority as participation, shifting from gatekeeping to connection and from institutional dependency to distributed capacity. The goal is no longer building organizations that need to remain at the center, but building structures strong enough that no one needs to own the movement at all.

Ultimately, the measure of a movement is not how powerful its leaders become, but how powerful its people become.

— JW

ADA Watch is a project of the Coalition for Disability Rights & Justice (CDRJ). We AMPLIFY the many voices of the disability rights & justice movement.

To Everyone Who Has Supported Me — Thank You.

Sometimes the words “thank you” don’t feel big enough to express the kind of gratitude I carry in my heart. But today, I just want to pause and speak from that space — the one filled with appreciation for each and every one of you who’s been part of my journey, whether loudly or quietly.

To my followers — the ones who’ve been here from the start, and those who just joined — thank you. Thank you for being present, for engaging with my content, for sharing it, for liking it, for commenting, and even for silently watching and supporting from a distance. Every click, every reaction, every message has meant more than you know.

Some of you share my work without tagging me. Some of you recommend me in rooms I haven’t entered. Some of you defend me in spaces I’ll never see. Some of you speak my name with respect when I’m not even in the conversation. And even though I may never hear those words directly — I feel them. And I appreciate you.
Then there are those of you who don’t follow me, but still show love. You don’t have to follow me to recognize my efforts, my growth, or my content. You support from the sidelines, and it still matters. Your support is just as powerful, just as appreciated, just as seen. Whether you’re a quiet observer or someone who occasionally engages — thank you. You’re part of the impact, and your energy adds to the momentum.

Support comes in many forms, and I’ve learned to appreciate every version of it. Some people show love loudly, others do it quietly — both are valid. Both are beautiful.

It’s easy to focus on numbers, algorithms, and growth — but none of that compares to the value of real support from real people. I don’t take it for granted. I know you don’t have to be here. I know you could scroll past. But you choose to be part of this space, this voice, this message — and that means everything.

To those who’ve reached out privately just to say, “Keep going” — you have no idea how those words land. Some of you have lifted my spirit without even realizing it. You’ve reminded me why I do what I do. Why I share. Why I stay consistent. Your encouragement fuels my resilience.

To those who have tagged their friends, told someone about my work, or shared my name in conversations — thank you. That kind of support is powerful. You’ve expanded my reach without asking for anything in return. You’ve amplified my voice simply because you believed in what I offer. That’s loyalty. That’s love.

To those who’ve never met me, but believe in me — I see you. It’s one thing to support someone you know. It’s another to support a stranger based on what they share, how they make you feel, or what they stand for. You don’t owe me anything, and yet you give your energy, attention, and kindness. I’m grateful for that.

I’ve grown so much — not just because of what I do, but because of the people around me who chose to believe in it. Because of those who didn’t just watch, but encouraged. Those who didn’t just consume, but connected. Those who didn’t just scroll, but stopped to say, “This matters.”

Your support isn’t just about helping me grow — it’s a reminder that what I say, what I create, and who I am has value. That I don’t need to change or shrink or water down. That being myself is enough. And that kind of validation — the organic, unforced kind — is priceless.

I’ve grown. I’ve glowed up — not just outside, but inside. I’ve unlearned the lies I once told myself and relearned the truth of who I am. I’ve walked away from what wasn’t serving me, even when it hurt. I’ve stood alone in rooms I once felt lost in, and found power in my own presence. I’ve cried. I’ve laughed. I’ve broken and rebuilt. Over and over.

There were days I didn’t believe in myself. But *someone* did. Maybe it was you. Maybe it was someone who shared my post. Maybe it was someone who said, “You inspire me.” Those moments matter. You matter.

I believe in divine timing now. I believe that everything and everyone comes into your life for a reason — to teach, to test, to heal, or to bless. And many of you, whether intentionally or not, have been a blessing. I’ve found encouragement in strangers, love in distant friends, and confidence in small milestones. That’s why I don’t take any of you for granted.

Every like, every share, every “Keep going” has helped me keep *showing up*. And for that, I thank you — deeply and honestly.

This journey has taught me that you don’t need to be famous to be impactful. You don’t need millions of followers to touch lives. Sometimes, just being real, being honest, being *you*… that’s enough.

So, if you’re reading this, and you’ve ever thought, “They don’t notice me,” — I do. Maybe not always by name, but by energy. I feel the love. I see the support. I carry it with me.

And this is not just about me — it’s about *us*.  
We’ve built something here.  
Something genuine.  
Something powerful.

I hope that when you see my posts, you feel inspired. Not because I’m perfect, but because I’m proof that *healing is possible, growth is real, and dreams are valid.*

I hope my words make you pause and reflect.  
I hope my heart reminds you that softness is strength.  
I hope my presence tells you: *you’re not alone.*

And if you’re in a season of uncertainty right now — I see you. Keep going. It’s okay to outgrow people, places, and versions of yourself. It’s okay to take breaks. To protect your peace. To choose yourself. Growth can be quiet. Healing can be slow. But both are beautiful.

As for me… I’m still becoming. I don’t have it all figured out. I’m still healing, still dreaming, still making sense of some parts of life. But I’ve made peace with that. I’ve stopped rushing the process. I’ve started trusting the pace. And most of all, I’ve started *trusting myself.*

So, this post isn’t just gratitude — it’s a celebration.  
Of growth.  
Of connection.

Of real people showing real love in a sometimes fake world.  

Whether we’ve known each other for years, months, or just a few scrolls — I thank you.  
If you’ve ever shared my words, laughed at my reels, related to my captions — I thank you.  
If you’ve ever whispered a prayer, told a friend, or simply sent good energy my way — I thank you.  

This space we’ve created together isn’t just about posts. It’s about purpose. It’s about healing, truth, love, and evolution. And I’m grateful to be on this journey with you.

To those who support in silence: you’re just as powerful.  
To those who cheer loudly: you’re just as appreciated.  
To those who are just observing: welcome — I hope you find what you didn’t know you were looking for.  

As I continue to grow, evolve, and step into higher versions of myself, I promise to keep showing up — with truth, with heart, with purpose.  
And I hope you keep walking with me.  

From my heart to yours:  
*Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.*

items.postText: I need help.  I was medically discharged in February 2005 from the US Navy after a heart condition become known during my time serving.  My file is an honorable discharge with a service connected disability that has a 0 rating.  The problem is I have so many more conditions that should be service connected and over the last 21 years they have steadily gotten worse.  Hiatal Hernia which causes sever GERD, causing so much pain that it is hard to sleep.  Diagnose sleep apnea, a constant ringing in my ears from my time on USS Abraham Lincoln and probably the worst is a back pain caused from an injury during a working party of all things.  Unloading pallets of boxes on our deployment caused a rib to pop out of joint which causes tissue damage all around my mid up and lower back.  This happens randomly now and will take me out for a full day or two of work when it happens.  I have almost exclusively used the VA for most medical issues but still don’t have any disability compensation and a 0 rating.  I need help filing my appeal to my original claim.  Anybody able to assist?
IBADAN LO MO O MO LAYIOPO.

I don't normally post about my personal life or situations... but this time I feel it's warranted. Because it’s personal, I was only going to post it for my subscribers, but seeing that I only have 2… 🤦🏻‍♂️ 

I was laid off from my job and I’ve been fighting like hell with the state of Arizona for unemployment. For some reason I kept getting denied. I didn’t understand how, being that I worked there for nearly 3 years.

2 appeals and 3 months later, I finally got approved. Like, literally JUST got approved within the last 2 weeks, after failing behind on EVERYTHING for 3 months. Fell behind on my rent, on all of my bills… my mid to high 700’s credit score, that I’ve worked so hard on, is completely ruined. I’ve got several judgements against me for non payment. My car insurance lapsed, causing a suspended registration, which immediately brings your license with it and suspends that too. 

I did what I could, when I could to find another job… but after a while with no cash, the gas tank dries up, and priorities change. Feeding my dogs became super high on my priority list, even above feeding myself. I have no family, no mom or dad, no siblings…  I’ve only been in Arizona for a few short years and making friends wasn’t really high up on my priority list either. 

So, this whole entire time, I’ve been fighting to get unemployment, which SHOULD HAVE kept me going immediately after losing my job, instead of leaving me stuck on a sinking ship, and now drowning in debt. I had spent hours upon hours, literally days and weeks of my life, on hold, on the phone, calling this state agency, calling that government agency, and I even physically drove to 3 different unemployment offices during my first 3 weeks after becoming unemployed. I was denied for EVERYTHING! Unemployment, nutrition assistance, housing assistance, financial assistance… almost everything I would’ve gotten instantly approved for if I didn’t have a license, birth certificate, and social security card… but I digress. 😒 

It wasn’t that my former employer kept denying me, it was the ID.me process through the Arizona state website that kept jamming me up. I wasn’t able to verify my identity, it wasn’t letting me. I was beyond frustrated, which was the root cause of me physically driving to those unemployment offices. 

This day and age, it’s beyond frustrating dealing with automated systems when all you want to do is speak to a LIVE representative. Nothing pisses me off more than Ai chat bots which, talk you around in circles, when there’s a problem that isn’t included on their pre programmed menus. They finally give you a number, where you’re then stuck dealing with ANOTHER automated system. 

T-Mobile, Chase Bank, AZ unemployment… everything is chat bots and automated systems, making it impossible to get a real person on the phone. But again, I digress… I’m getting off topic. 

Like I said, after 3 months, and on my second appeal I finally got approved. Upon approval, they make you wait another entire week before you can even START getting the measly amount of benefits that they allow. During that “waiting week” the state of Arizona sent me a letter, which I just received on Saturday, that has me absolutely furious and totally beside myself.  

I received a letter from AZDES, which is the Arizona Department of Economic Security, telling me that I need to provide PROOF that I’m no longer receiving any government assistance IN CALIFORNIA!!! 🤬 

I do not live in California. I have never been to California. I have never worked in California. And I don’t even know anyone who lives in California. 

Apparently, I have been receiving government assistance in California for the last 26 months. I’ve been receiving SNAP benefits, welfare checks, and a housing allowance. It’s not section 8, but a California program that pays 3/4’s of your rent directly to a landlord, as part of some homelessness prevention program. 

I am absolutely livid!!! 😤 Just over 2 years ago, someone in California had used MY social security number, went on the California state website, and signed up for a bunch of programs using JUST my social security number. 

The last couple of days I’ve been trying to play detective, to see how much information I can get, because I need SOMETHING! How tf can I prove to Arizona that I’m not getting something that I was never involved with in the first place? The department of economic security also wants me to prove that I’m no longer working at a job that I’ve had. So I started with that. 

I tried looking this place up in California, and big surprise, it doesn’t exist. Someone signed up for government assistance saying that they worked at a job for LESS THAN minimum wage, just to be able to get approved for everything. 

I went on the California State website and it told me that I needed an account, that I don’t have, and don’t even know the email associated. I got to a point where it found MY “account” after using a search with my social security number. Now, even though it’s MY social security number, it sent the password reset and login information to the email address associated with MY Social Security number. 🤦🏻‍♂️ 

I used the chat bots and automated systems after every single contact phone number I could find. I’m beyond pissed! Not only did I have to go through all this BS with Arizona, but now it’s the SAME BS with California. My life has been swirling around the toilet for 3 months, about to get flushed away, and this stupid azz Ai chat bot wants to know the exact reason for my issue so it can direct me to the right department, then tells I have to log into my account, an account I CANNOT get or create because my social security number is already linked to someone else’s account. 😡 

After 3 days of trying, I FINALLY got a live person on the phone. I tried to explain the situation the best I could to the woman on the phone with a THICH Spanish accent, who spoke extremely fast, and I couldn’t, for the life of me, understand what she was saying. First off, I felt like she was barely paying attention to me. Second, I had to keep asking her to repeat herself because I just couldn’t understand her… but this is what God gave me, this was the hand I was dealt, and I do NOT have another 3 days to waste trying to get someone else on the phone. I could tell she was getting progressively more frustrated with me also. Every time I asked her to repeat herself, she would suck her teeth and let out a loud, audible sigh of disgust. Like, sorry I don’t speak Spanish, but seriously WTF?!!! 

I’m sure you’re all going to love this as much as I did: in California, YOU DONT NEED A PHOTO ID to sign up for these government programs!! I tried asking for the name and address that was on the account and she refused to give it to me. I tried explaining over and over again that it’s MY social security number that’s being used. I even got her work email address (which was a job in itself) and i literally sent her a picture of my original social security card and the original sheet it was attached to, along with the letter than came with directly from the social security administration. I sent her a picture of my photo ID and my birth certificate. After all this, she tells me that MY name, on MY social security card doesn’t match the name that she has on file, so she can’t give me any information. 😡🤬😤

California’s great laws and policies will give anybody, anything, without an ID… but yet here I am WITH an ID, trying to prove to this person who I am, and explain that whoever is getting those benefits is a fkn fraud! 😡 Again, I am beyond pissed off at this whole situation. 

Back to my original problem. How can I PROVE to the state of Arizona that I’m NOT getting something that I NEVER got, and I’m NOT working at a job that I NEVER had? And how can I do all of this NOW? Not now, but RIGHT NOW, before I’m consumed by debt, completely drown, and get evicted? I seriously NEED these benefits and assistance, that I feel I’ve earned after being a taxpayer for more than 20 years, and having never needed them before. I’m seriously about to lose everything. It’s so frustrating and discouraging. You work and do the right thing for so long… and then when there’s a situation beyond your control and you need help, some dipsh!t’s policies in another state just gives that help to someone else without ever checking on who they are. 

Governor Gavin Newsom I thought you were all for the “working class”? I’m working class and you screwed me! I don’t even live in your jacked up state and you screwed me. I’m about to lose everything because you want to give everything away to people without a single care or concern for who they are, or if they’re even in this country legally! How many OTHER people, outside of California, are getting screwed the same exact way because of YOUR policies? 

The sad part is, in both the AZ & CA websites, it asks you about immigration status and has an option that still allows you to sign up. So if I didn’t even have a social security number, wasn’t an American citizen, didn’t have a birth certificate or green card… it would’ve expedited the whole process and approved me on the spot! 😡 

Oh, and here’s the kicker… I made sure to ask her, and the only information she WAS allowed to give me: I’m a registered DEMOCRAT voter in California! Which now makes sense as to why I received a letter from the Az board of elections about 2 weeks after I voted in the 2024 presidential election, saying there was a discrepancy with my ballot￼, and asking me to prove my address.
This.

Dear Aetna Insurance,
My daughter was diagnosed with Adult Atypical Cystic Fibrosis. She has a rare mutation which makes it even more difficult to treat. She has been fighting the battle for far too long. We are grateful that she is in the care of an incredible team of medical professionals at Brigham&Woman’s and Beth Israel in Boston. They are some of the best. While we are aware there is no cure and that treatment is often difficult, her team gave us all a flicker of hope for improvement with the potential of a type of infusion therapy. We are fully aware that this therapy won’t fix the problem but we sure were hopeful at the thought of improvement of her symptoms and maybe, just maybe, an improved quality of life, but more so, some relief for her in this battle. That flicker of hope was quickly diminished when you denied the claim for treatment. Yes, she will appeal, yes, she will fight, she’s been fighting this disease for years, fighting is all she knows. But, as a mom, I ask you, and your millionaire  president, Mr. Steve Nelson, when you post this statement on your website…”We’re always working to push health care forward as a true partner. As part of CVS Health®, we’re building on this legacy to help people achieve their personal health goals in new and unique ways” to please, please stand behind your statement. Work as a partner in health to help my daughter, (and anyone needing rare treatments), get better, or at the very least, give her a shot a better quality of life. This rare mutation is new and unique, and this treatment might just help her achieve her health goals. All the things you say on your website is all we are asking. I’m 100% certain if it was your child, you would want the same.
Sincerely,
A mom that is broken watching her child get sicker and sicker.

Magun: Please pee in my mouth and save me
By Funke Egbemode

The news from Osun was bizarre, even by Nigerian standards.

A man was reportedly dying on the street. Those around him apparently believed he had encountered magun, an ancient Yoruba nightmare whose name roughly translates to “do not climb”. Magun is believed to be an instant killer, but this particular Osun instance had a solution.

The woman suspected to be the magun victim’s partner-in-sin should urinate in his mouth.

Ah.

There are deaths.

There are embarrassing deaths.

And then there are deaths where your alleged last hope is standing over you, saying, tragically,

“I don’t know this man.”

According to eyewitness accounts (in Yoruba) on social media, the woman refused. She reportedly denied being his lover. The desperate man begged. People around cursed and shouted.

The woman stood her ground.

“I don’t know him.”

My people, imagine climbing a fence with somebody and, when the DisCo cuts off the light while you’re still on top, your fellow climber suddenly says she has never seen you before.

This is why every business needs an exit strategy, especially illegal businesses.

Now, before somebody sends for the village herbalist to start a lecture on the origins of magun, let us establish something important. Magun belongs to Yoruba traditional belief and folklore. Researchers have documented beliefs in different varieties and supposed consequences, but that is not scientific proof that a charm caused any particular death. Sudden collapse during or after sex can have medical explanations, including cardiac arrest. That is why a woman cannot be accused of murder just because a man somersaults in her bed. Magun is not captured in our law books. Viewed from another angle, if your neighbour collapses, please call for medical help. Don’t form an emergency committee and start looking for urine.

That said, Yoruba folklore surrounding magun is enough to make a wandering husband reconsider his extracurricular timetable.

Because, according to tradition, magun does not come in one flavour.

There is reportedly má jè ìlà — don’t eat okro. Accounts of Yoruba traditional belief indeed identify an okro-associated form among the varieties.

Which means from today, ladies, when a perfectly healthy Yoruba man announces:

“I don’t eat okro.”

Don’t accuse him of anything.

Just look at him with side eyes, from head to toe. Then ask: “Since when?”

If he starts sweating before the soup arrives, I have said nothing.

Maybe he simply dislikes okro. Maybe.

There are also traditional accounts of varieties associated with water or particular prohibitions. The wider literature on magun stresses that its alleged forms, effects and antidotes vary considerably from practitioner to practitioner and community to community.

Our elders clearly believed that if a man insisted on inspecting another man’s compound, ordinary “no trespassing” signs were insufficient.

They allegedly installed spiritual CCTV.

Imagine living under a taboo that says don’t cross a river.

In Yorubaland?

Where will you go?

Your girlfriend says, “Darling, come to my village.”

You ask, “Any river?”

She says, “Just one small bridge.”

The relationship ends immediately.

“It’s not you, Bose. I need to work on myself.”

Work on yourself, really?

You are avoiding Osun River.

Then there is the one popularly described as the somersaulting magun.

This is the heavyweight champion of the belief.

Traditional accounts say the offending lover may somersault repeatedly—often described as three times—before dying.

Three!

Not one warning somersault so you can repent.

No VAR.

No appeal.

No Supreme Court.

According to the folklore, once the performance starts, the curtain closes.

And this is where my sympathy begins to develop a puncture.

Because why are you climbing another man’s fence in the first place?

Millions of unattached women walk around peacefully.

But no.

Some men see “married” and apparently read: Special offer.

Then there is the alleged urine remedy—the particularly humiliating version at the centre of this Osun story.

Imagine the negotiations.

“Please, save me!”

“Who? Do I know you?”

“Ah, Ajike”

“I don’t know him.”

“Moji, this is not a joke.”

Neighbours have gathered now.

Phones are recording.

Your ancestors are probably changing surnames.

And your supposed lover—the co-defendant in the matter—is insisting she has never met you since God created heaven and earth.

That is not merely heartbreak.

That is abandonment at the scene of the crime.

But beneath the laughter is something worth saying.

Adultery has always carried risks, with or without magun. Broken homes. Violence. Sexually transmitted infections. Public disgrace. Blackmail. Emotional wreckage. And, in some circumstances, medical emergencies.

You don’t need to believe in thunderbolts to understand consequences.

And you certainly should not watch a person convulsing, collapsing or struggling to breathe and conclude that what he needs is a bowl, a volunteer and fresh urine.

Get him medical help.

Let the doctors first deal with what science can establish.

If the family wants to discuss ancestors afterward, that meeting can hold when everybody is alive.

Still, Yoruba people knew how to name things.

Magun.

Don’t climb.

Two words.

No long sermon.

No PowerPoint presentation.

No marriage seminar.

Just:

Don’t. Climb.

Perhaps modern men require the updated version:

Dear Sir,

That fence you are admiring has an owner.

You do not know what is behind it.

You don’t know whether there is an angry husband, CCTV, disease, scandal, violence—or merely the spectacular humiliation of discovering at your hour of greatest need that your beloved co-conspirator has developed acute amnesia.

And if you are one of those gentlemen who mysteriously doesn’t eat okro, doesn’t drink gari, avoids rivers and becomes nervous whenever somebody mentions somersaulting…

My brother.

We are not accusing you.

We just want to know: exactly how many people’s fences have you been climbing?
