When Grace Offends Us

There is a sentence buried inside nearly every objection to Christian forgiveness that sounds morally serious until you slow down and listen to what it is actually saying. It usually appears when the conversation reaches the worst kinds of human evil, the acts we cannot discuss without feeling something inside us recoil. The murderer should not be forgiven. The rapist should not be forgiven. The person who brutalized another human being does not deserve forgiveness. That last sentence is the one worth holding onto, because it is entirely true. He does not deserve forgiveness. The mistake is believing that anyone else does.

Forgiveness that is deserved is not forgiveness. It is compensation. It is something owed to a person who has satisfied the necessary conditions and earned the right to receive it. The gospel begins by removing that possibility from the room. “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). Paul does not flatten every sin into the same earthly consequence, and neither should we. Murder is not identical to an angry thought. Abuse is not identical to impatience. Some sins tear through the lives of other people and leave wounds that may remain until the resurrection, and any theology that asks the wounded to call that damage insignificant is not the theology of Scripture. But beneath every difference in severity stands one unchanging fact. No sinner possesses a claim upon the mercy of God.

The respectable man and the condemned criminal may not be equally destructive to their neighbors, but neither can stand before a holy God and demand forgiveness as something he has earned. That is where the offense of grace actually begins. It does not begin with the claim that a murderer can be forgiven. It begins with the claim that you need the same kind of mercy he does. The ground at the foot of the cross is level, not because every sinner has committed the same sins, but because no sinner can climb high enough to reach God without Christ coming down to save him. We are willing to speak of grace as long as it remains an encouragement for people like us. We begin to object when grace reaches the person whose guilt we cannot bear to look at. Somewhere inside us, we have divided the human race into sinners who need mercy and monsters who have surrendered the right to receive it. Scripture knows nothing of that division. It gives us guilty people and a Savior who loses none of those the Father has given him.

That does not make the outrage against evil wrong. There is something right in the refusal to treat cruelty as a small thing. A human being made in the image of God has been violated, and the instinct that cries out for justice is not an enemy of Christianity. It is evidence that we know, even when we cannot fully explain why, that some things deserve condemnation. The mistake comes when we assume that God can forgive only by becoming less just than we are. We imagine forgiveness as a shrug from heaven, as if God surveys the blood, the fear, the betrayal, and the years of suffering that follow and decides that none of it finally matters. But the God of Scripture never calls evil good, never confuses darkness with light, and never clears the guilty by pretending they were innocent all along. Christian forgiveness does not begin with God lowering his standard. It begins with God satisfying it.

Paul takes us into the heart of that mystery when he says that God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25). That word reaches deeper than the idea that Jesus simply showed us how much God loves us. Christ stood beneath the righteous judgment our sins deserved and exhausted it in the place of his people. Paul says this happened “to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). God does not choose mercy instead of justice. He remains just while justifying the ungodly because the sentence has been carried out upon a willing substitute. The cross is not the abandonment of moral order. It is the place where the moral perfection of God is displayed with a severity no human court could ever approach.

This is why the cross will not allow us to speak lightly about sin. If forgiveness required nothing more than divine tolerance, Gethsemane makes no sense. The thorns make no sense. The darkness over Calvary makes no sense. The cry of dereliction makes no sense. The eternal Son took to himself a true human nature, obeyed the law we had broken, stood in the place of sinners, and drank the cup of judgment down to its last bitter drop. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). The Father did not look away from evil. He judged it. The Son did not excuse the guilty. He bore their guilt. God did not lower the price of forgiveness until wicked people could afford it. Christ paid everything justice demanded because none of us could pay any part of it.

But the cross did more than cancel a debt and leave the sinner standing at zero, forgiven but empty-handed. Christ lived the life God required and we failed to live, loving the Father with all his heart through every moment of his earthly obedience, fulfilling every command we have broken a thousand times, and doing it all as the last Adam standing where the first Adam fell. When Paul says that God made him “to be sin,” he says in the same breath that we become “the righteousness of God” in him. That is not just the absence of guilt. It is the presence of a righteousness that is not our own, credited to us as fully as though we had lived Christ’s obedience ourselves. The believing sinner does not stand before God as one who has only been acquitted. He stands clothed. The judgment Christ bore on the cross removes the wrath we deserved, and the righteousness Christ accomplished through every day of his obedient life is counted as ours. Both sides of that exchange belong to the gospel, nothing can be removed without leaving the sinner with less than Christ came to give.

There is a voice behind the objection we started with, and Scripture names it plainly. Satan is “the accuser of our brothers,” the one who “accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10). He does not always need to invent his accusations. He points toward real guilt and insists that the record must remain in force, that the guilty must stay guilty, and that mercy shown to the worst sinner would somehow be an injustice against everyone watching. Our resistance to mercy can begin with a proper concern for justice, especially when the wounds are real and the offender has never shown repentance. But it begins to echo the accuser when it insists that even the blood of Christ must not be allowed to answer certain sins.

The cross satisfied the law and silenced the accuser. Paul says that God, having forgiven us all our trespasses, canceled “the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands” and set it aside, nailing it to the cross, and in that same act “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:14–15). The writer to the Hebrews says Christ took on flesh and blood so that “through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). The resurrection was not simply the Father’s public declaration that the sacrifice had been accepted. It was the announcement of a battle won. The one who wanted to hold sinners beneath their record no longer possesses any accusation that can stand against those who are in Christ. When the accuser points toward the sins of someone Christ has claimed and insists that the debt is too great for grace, he is citing a debt that has already been paid and appealing a verdict that will never be overturned.

There is a strange contradiction in the modern objection to the gospel at this point. People insist that a loving God must forgive them without requiring atonement, but they also insist that there are other people he must never forgive at all. They want mercy without a cross for themselves and justice without mercy for their enemies. The gospel refuses both demands. It tells us that our sins are worse than we have allowed ourselves to believe, because nothing less than the death of Christ could answer for them. It also tells us that his grace is greater than we have dared to imagine, because no guilt remains unconquerable when Christ has borne it. The same cross that closes the mouth of the self-righteous opens the door of hope to the worst sinner who comes to Jesus empty-handed.

That is the part that offends us. We do not mind a grace that helps decent people become better. We can even admire a grace that gives someone a second chance after an understandable failure. What unsettles us is grace that enters a prison cell, grace that reaches bloodstained hands, grace that finds someone after he has destroyed lives he can never repair. We feel as though mercy shown to the offender must somehow be taken away from the victim, as if God has only enough righteousness to defend one or enough compassion to love the other. But divine justice and divine mercy are not competing needs inside God. At the cross, God condemns sin more completely than we ever could and saves the sinner more completely than we ever would.

Manasseh forces us to face this. Second Kings tells us that he rebuilt the high places, practiced sorcery, filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and even burned his son as an offering. He was not a basically decent man who wandered into a difficult season. He used power to corrupt a nation and destroy human lives. Yet when judgment came and he was taken captive, Second Chronicles says that “he entreated the favor of the Lord his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers” (2 Chronicles 33:12). God heard him and restored him. That mercy did not rewrite Manasseh’s history or make the blood he shed less real. It displayed something Manasseh could never have displayed through self-improvement, which is the immeasurable depth of the mercy of God toward a sinner who had no remaining argument in his own defense.

Saul of Tarsus brings the offense even closer to the church. He did not just disagree with Christians. He entered house after house, dragged men and women away, approved the killing of Stephen, and tried to destroy the people of Christ. If you had stood beside the families he shattered, Saul’s conversion might not have felt like good news at first. It may have felt like God had allowed the persecutor to escape what he deserved. But Saul did not escape justice because justice fell upon Christ, and the mercy that pardoned Saul did not leave Saul untouched. The man who once breathed threats and murder spent the rest of his life suffering to proclaim the Christ he had hated. Grace did not declare that his persecution was harmless. Grace conquered the persecutor.

Paul never forgot what he had been, but he also refused to make his past more powerful than Christ. “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Timothy 1:15). He did not say that to turn his former violence into a dramatic testimony or to keep himself beneath a sentence Jesus had already borne. He said it because his life had become an exhibit of divine patience. “But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience” (1 Timothy 1:16). The point was not that Paul had discovered a religious method for reinventing himself. The point was that the risen Christ had claimed his enemy, given him a new heart, and made him an apostle of the gospel he once tried to silence.

Manasseh had years left to show that grace had changed him. Saul had decades left to spend proclaiming the Christ he once hated. The thief on the cross beside Jesus was given neither. He could not descend from his cross and repair what he had done. He admitted that his sentence was just and that Jesus had done nothing wrong. Then he turned toward the dying King and said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Jesus answered, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The thief brought no lifetime of obedience, no opportunity to rebuild his reputation, and no future works with which to prove himself. He brought guilt, need, and a dying appeal to Christ. Jesus gave him paradise because salvation rests upon the worthiness of the Savior, not the worthiness of the sinner.

The thief still died on his cross, a divine pardon did not require the Roman soldiers to remove the earthly consequence of his crime. His broken body remained beneath judgment in this world while his soul was received by Christ into glory. That scene guards us from two opposite errors. It will not allow us to make earthly consequences the price of divine forgiveness, because Christ freely saved a man who could do nothing to repair his past. It will not allow us to use divine forgiveness as proof that earthly consequences no longer matter, because the forgiven thief still completed his sentence. Grace did not make justice meaningless. Grace gave a condemned man a kingdom no human court could grant and no Roman nail could keep him from entering.

These three men came to mercy by very different roads, but none of their stories can be explained by native human willingness. Manasseh did not lift himself out of rebellion. God brought him low through judgment until the king who had refused to hear was humbled enough to cry for mercy. Saul did not travel toward Damascus searching for Jesus. He was going there to arrest Christians when Christ appeared to him, named him, stopped him, and turned him around. Even the thief’s dying appeal came while the sinless King was being crucified beside him, near enough to be heard because providence had placed him there. Behind every true coming to Christ stands the grace of God awakening what sin had left dead.

Paul does not describe election as God choosing an undefined class and then waiting to see which sinners will place themselves inside it. He says the Father “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). God chose definite sinners, but he did not choose them to remain isolated names scattered across eternity. He chose them together in Christ as one covenant people, a flock given to its Shepherd, a bride promised to her Bridegroom, and a body that would be joined to its Head. That does not mean the elect were already vitally united to Christ before they were born. They were chosen in Christ from eternity and are united to Christ in time when the Spirit calls them through the gospel. Election determines that union and guarantees it, but the Spirit still applies it personally to every sinner the Father has given the Son.

Election and condemnation are not two equal faces of the same coin. In election, God reaches into spiritual death and creates life where no life existed and no mercy was owed. He gives faith, repentance, righteousness, adoption, and every grace necessary to bring the sinner safely into glory. The lost are not forced into unbelief by God or made sinful by a corresponding work of damnation. He leaves them in the rebellion they already love, and he judges them for sins that are truly their own. God’s decree encompasses both outcomes, but he does not stand behind belief and unbelief in the same way.

Salvation is the fruit of sovereign mercy. Condemnation is the execution of perfect justice. If God rescued no one, no one would receive less than he deserved. The wonder is not that God leaves some guilty sinners beneath judgment. The wonder is that he chose to rescue any of us at all.

Jesus says, “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). No one who comes to Christ will ever be told that his sin was too great or that mercy has run out. But Jesus also explains why anyone comes at all. “All that the Father gives me will come to me,” and he promises that he will lose none of them (John 6:37–39). The Father did not give the Son an unnamed possibility. He gave him a people. “I lay down my life for the sheep,” Jesus says (John 10:15), and Paul writes that “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). The Shepherd died for his flock. The Bridegroom purchased his bride. The Head gave himself for his body.

The gospel offer goes out honestly to everyone who hears it, and everyone who comes will be received. But the reason the worst sinner ever comes is not that he found a spiritual willingness hidden somewhere inside himself. It is that the Shepherd came looking for him.

Coming to Christ is more than becoming aware that we need help. A man can know that he is guilty, understand the facts of the cross, agree that Jesus rose from the dead, and still refuse to bow before him. Saving faith is not bare knowledge, and it is not admiration from a safe distance. It is the empty-handed sinner casting himself upon Christ with nothing left to negotiate and no rival claim to preserve. Jesus does not offer himself simply as a way to escape punishment while we continue governing our own lives. He comes as Savior and Lord, and we do not make him Lord by submitting to him. We submit because he is Lord already. The gospel summons us to repent and believe, to abandon every claim of self-righteousness, and to lay ourselves at the foot of the cross beneath the rule of the King who died and rose to save us.

Even that surrender is not something the natural heart produces from its own untouched resources. The sinner does not conquer his rebellion and then present his submission to Christ as the final contribution that completes salvation. He still possesses the natural faculties of mind and will. He can hear the gospel, understand its claims, make choices, speak religious words, and perform outwardly religious acts. His inability is not the absence of a human will. It is the bondage of a will that loves darkness and refuses the Christ it was created to worship. Jesus says, “Yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life” (John 5:40). The problem is not that the sinner has no will. The problem is that the will he has is governed by a heart hostile to God.

He does not need the Spirit to create a different kind of human mind or give him a faculty he never possessed. He needs the Spirit to give him a new heart, renew his mind, and liberate his will from its bondage to sin. The Spirit opens blind eyes, removes the heart of stone, and makes the unwilling sinner willing to come. Paul says, “No one can say ‘Jesus is Lord’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). The Spirit does not drag the sinner to Christ while leaving him unchanged in his hatred. He changes the sinner’s heart so that the sinner sees Christ as beautiful, comes freely, and lays down the weapons he once raised against him. Faith receives Christ because grace has awakened the heart to receive him. Repentance turns from sin because the Spirit has shown the sinner the ugliness of the old master and the glory of the new one.

The claim that if everyone can be forgiven, everyone may as well do anything is not a new objection. Paul heard it in the first century, and he did not answer it by adding human merit to grace. “What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?” (Romans 6:1–2). The gospel does not give the old man permission to live more comfortably. It declares that the old man has been crucified with Christ. Forgiveness is not a permission slip handed to someone who intends to remain exactly what he was. Christ does not forgive the old life so that it can continue without fear of judgment. He brings that life to the cross, raises the sinner into newness of life, and claims the whole person for himself.

The new birth that makes faith and repentance possible is not a religious adjustment made to the old life. It is resurrection. God does not educate the old man until he becomes slightly more manageable. He puts the old man to death with Christ and raises a new creation to walk in newness of life. “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). The water is not the author of that resurrection. The Spirit is. Baptism is the God-appointed sacramental sign of union with Christ, declaring publicly the death and resurrection Christ has accomplished and the Spirit has applied. This is why baptism follows repentance and faith so closely in the ordinary pattern of Scripture. It does not create the new birth, but it belongs at the threshold of the new life as “an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:21).

Regeneration itself is not gradual or partial. It is the decisive act of God by which the sinner who was spiritually dead is made alive, the heart of stone is replaced with a heart of flesh, and a new life begins where no life existed before. The Christian is not instantly sinless, but he is genuinely different. Sin remains present, but it no longer reigns as his unquestioned master.

That difference will not appear with the same speed or strength in every believer. Some sins fall away quickly. Others must be fought across years of prayer, discipline, failure, confession, and renewed dependence upon the Spirit. The evidence of new birth is not flawless performance. It is a new direction, a new allegiance, and a new war where there was once only surrender to sin. The regenerate person still sins, but he can no longer make peace with sin. He grieves it, confesses it, turns from it, and returns again to the Christ whose finished work remains his only righteousness. He may stumble on the new road, sometimes painfully and even grievously, but he cannot settle permanently into the old road as though Christ had never found him. He walks a new path, not because his steps are perfect, but because the Shepherd has made him alive, called him by name, and is leading him somewhere he would never have gone on his own.

The Spirit does not bring a dead heart to life and then leave the new creature to continue by the strength of the flesh. The finished work of Christ does not simply make forgiveness possible and leave sanctification for us to complete. The same Savior who bore our guilt purchased every grace necessary to conform us to his image, and the Spirit applies that finished work throughout the whole Christian life. Paul tells believers to “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,” but he does not leave the source of that obedience in doubt. “For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13). We work because God is working in us. We obey with our minds, our wills, our hands, and our feet, but beneath every act of genuine obedience is the grace of God creating both the desire and the strength to do what pleases him.

That does not make the Christian passive. The Spirit does not replace our obedience. He produces it and carries us through it. We put sin to death, but we do it “by the Spirit” (Romans 8:13). We strive for holiness, but we do so with strength supplied by God rather than attempting to finish by the flesh what the Spirit began. Paul describes the whole Christian life when he writes, “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Sanctification is not self-salvation stretched across the remainder of the Christian life. It is the risen Christ, through his indwelling Spirit, changing those he has already justified so that day by day they increasingly resemble the One who saved them.

This is why repentance cannot be separated from forgiveness even though repentance never purchases it. Repentance is not a payment offered to God or a moral achievement added to the blood of Christ. It is the sinner’s Spirit-given turning from sin to the Savior. The person who says he has been forgiven while defending his cruelty, silencing his victims, and continuing in the same unrepentant pattern is not displaying the freedom of grace. He is using Christian language to hide from the light. John the Baptist did not tell people to speak convincingly about repentance. He said, “Bear fruits in keeping with repentance” (Luke 3:8). A changed life is not the cause of justification, but it is the necessary fruit of the new birth. The tree does not live because it bears fruit. It bears fruit because it lives.

That fruit includes confession without manipulation. It includes accepting consequences without pretending that forgiveness makes accountability unnecessary. It includes restitution where restitution is possible, submission to the discipline of the church, and a willingness to surrender positions of trust that can no longer be held safely. Zacchaeus did not respond to grace by telling the people he had defrauded that they were obligated to forget. He said, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8). Jesus did not teach that restitution purchased salvation. He declared that salvation had come to the house, and the opened hands of Zacchaeus showed that grace had reached the heart.

This distinction matters because the language of forgiveness has sometimes been used to place another burden upon people who have already been wounded. A victim is told that if she has truly forgiven, she must act as though nothing happened. She must immediately trust the person who deceived her, return to the person who harmed her, or remain silent so that his reputation can be protected. That is not biblical forgiveness. Forgiveness does not require a lie about danger. It does not remove the magistrate’s duty to punish crime, the church’s duty to exercise discipline, or a parent’s duty to protect a child. Romans 13 does not call the civil authority “the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer” and then instruct him to abandon justice whenever the wrongdoer claims grace. God may forgive a murderer eternally while the state still carries out a temporal sentence. Those truths do not contradict each other because civil justice and justification before God answer different questions.

Forgiveness is not identical to reconciliation either. Forgiveness releases personal vengeance and refuses to make hatred a permanent home in the heart. Reconciliation is the restoration of fellowship, and Scripture never constructs that restoration upon denial, coercion, or continued unrepentance. Jesus says, “If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him” (Luke 17:3). Repentance does not make the offender worthy of grace, but it makes truthful reconciliation possible because the evil is no longer being defended. Trust may return slowly, and in some relationships it may never return in its former shape. The wounds may be forgiven without the old access being restored. A victim can entrust final vengeance to God, pray for an enemy, and refuse to be ruled by bitterness while also locking the door, calling the police, telling the truth, and never again placing herself or her children within that person’s reach.

Elders carry a particular weight here, and they should not hide from it behind the general call to forgive. When a wounded believer brings her story to those who shepherd her, Scripture does not ask them to weigh her safety against the offender’s reputation as though those concerns possessed equal moral weight. Paul tells those who are spiritual to restore a sinning brother, but the same verse warns each restorer to “keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Galatians 6:1). Restoration must therefore be handled with humility, vigilance, and no room for the pride, partiality, or self-protection that can distort judgment. Peter charges elders to shepherd the flock without “domineering over those in your charge” (1 Peter 5:2–3). Pastoral authority must never be used to pressure a victim toward reconciliation before repentance has made truthful reconciliation possible. An eldership that rushes the process to protect a man’s standing or preserve the church’s reputation has confused the appearance of unity with the substance of holiness, and it has asked the wounded to carry a burden Christ never placed upon them.

There is something else beneath our resistance that is harder to admit. Sometimes we object to mercy for great sinners because we believe our own lesser sins have placed God in our debt. We have not murdered, abused, or brutalized anyone, and we quietly turn those things into evidence that we deserve a warmer welcome. We compare ourselves horizontally and call the distance between our conduct and someone else’s conduct righteousness. Jesus told a parable about a Pharisee who did exactly that. “God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers” (Luke 18:11). Everything he said about his public conduct may have been true. The problem was that he had made another man’s wickedness the measure of his own standing before God.

The tax collector had no such speech. He would not even lift his eyes to heaven. He beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Jesus says that man went home justified rather than the other. The difference was not that the tax collector’s sins did not matter. The difference was that he had stopped presenting himself as a man who deserved acceptance and cast himself upon mercy. The Pharisee wanted a verdict based upon comparison. The tax collector asked for propitiation. One stood near the things of God while trusting himself, and the other stood far off while depending entirely upon grace. Only one of them understood the room he was standing in.

If you believe there are people who do not deserve forgiveness, you have finally said something true about the whole human race. That truth was never meant to leave you staring at the sins of other people. It was meant to bring you to the place where the tax collector stood. You may never have committed the crimes that awaken public horror, and gratitude for restraining grace should keep you from pretending that you have. But you have loved created things more than the Creator. You have spoken words you cannot retrieve, hidden motives you would not want exposed, withheld love when it was owed, and carried private rebellions beneath a respectable exterior. The law does not need to accuse you of someone else’s sin. It knows your name, your history, your secrets, and the precise weight of every command you have broken. It moves through the conscience like a searchlight through a darkened room, exposing what was hoping to remain in the corner. Nothing stays hidden beneath its light, but the law can expose the disease without providing the cure. For that, you need the gospel.

That is where the gospel meets you. It does not meet you at the top of a ladder you have climbed more successfully than the people beneath you. It meets you on the ground, without leverage, without payment, without any remaining claim that God must receive you because you are not as bad as someone else. Jesus Christ lived the righteous life you have not lived. He bore the judgment your sin deserves. He rose bodily from the grave, breaking the dominion of death, and he now receives every sinner who comes to him in repentance and faith. The promise of John 6 is wide enough for the criminal you despise and personal enough for the guilt you hide. Everyone the Father gives to the Son will come, everyone who comes will be received, and everyone Christ receives will be kept.

The church must learn to hold all of this together because the world rarely does. We must be a people who name evil truthfully, protect the vulnerable immediately, report crimes honestly, practice discipline faithfully, and refuse to confuse cheap words with repentance. We must also be a people who believe that the blood of Christ can cleanse the worst sinner and that the Spirit of God can create a new heart where no human possibility of change remains. If we defend justice without grace, we will become a community in which sinners learn to hide. If we speak of grace without justice, we will become a community in which victims are asked to disappear. The cross permits neither. It brings hidden things into the light, condemns evil without qualification, shelters the wounded, humbles the self-righteous, and offers real pardon to everyone who takes refuge in Christ.

The Word keeps that balance before us because the Word will not let us edit God into the image of our instincts. It will not let the guilty call sin a mistake when God calls it rebellion. It will not let the proud call themselves righteous when God says there is none righteous, no, not one. It will not let the wounded believe that God is indifferent to what was done to them, and it will not let the offender believe that his guilt extends beyond the reach of Christ. Week after week, the preached gospel strips away both despair and presumption. It tells the unrepentant sinner that he cannot have Christ while making peace with the sin for which Christ died. It tells the broken sinner that he does not have to cleanse himself before coming to the fountain, because the blood that cleanses is not his own.

The Lord’s Table places that gospel before the church in bread and the cup. No one approaches that Table because he deserves a place there. We come confessing that the body of Christ was given for sinners and that his blood established the covenant in which forgiveness is not imagined but secured. The person beside you may have a past you would struggle to hear, and you may carry wounds no one in the room can see. Yet the Table does not say that those histories are unimportant. It says that the only hope for either of you is the crucified and risen Christ, received by faith, who feeds his people with the grace he purchased for them, both the pardon secured by his blood and the perfect righteousness he accomplished through his obedience. The victim is not asked to call evil good. The repentant offender is not asked to make himself clean. Both are directed away from themselves to the Lamb of God who takes away sin.

One day the distinction between hidden guilt and public guilt will disappear. Every secret thing will be brought into judgment, every disguise will fall, and every human being will stand before the King. On that day, no one will accuse God of caring too little about justice. Every unrepentant sin will receive its exact and righteous sentence, and every wrong that was ignored by earthly courts will be answered by the Judge who cannot be bribed, deceived, or intimidated. The Christian hope is not that God will finally decide sin did not matter. It is that all sin will be judged, either in the sinner or in the substitute who stood in the sinner’s place. There will be no unpaid account in the kingdom of God.

This is why grace can be offered without fear that the moral order will collapse. Grace does not erase the holiness of God. It reveals it. Grace does not teach that anyone may do whatever he pleases because forgiveness is available. Grace takes a slave of sin, unites him to Christ, gives him a new heart, places the Holy Spirit within him, and begins conforming him to the image of the One who saved him. That change is not produced by the sinner attempting to repay Christ for salvation. It is the continuing work of Christ within someone whose salvation has already been purchased and secured. Grace does not remove every temporal consequence or instantly repair everything the sinner destroyed. It does something no punishment or human determination could ever accomplish. It reconciles the guilty to God, makes the enemy a son, and then works within that son until the family likeness begins to appear.

You may still feel the resistance rise when you imagine that mercy reaching someone whose sins disgust you. Do not rush past that feeling. Let it show you how easily you can believe that grace belongs to you as a possession rather than coming to you as a gift. Then look at the cross until every illusion of deserving has been taken away. The man who brutalized another person does not deserve forgiveness. The murderer does not deserve forgiveness. The abuser does not deserve forgiveness. Neither do I, and neither do you. That is not the weakness of the Christian gospel. That is the reason it is good news.

Jesus does not save good people who finally earn his attention. He saves the ungodly. He does not excuse what they have done, bargain with his Father for a reduced sentence, or wave evil away with a sentimental word about love. He takes their guilt as his own, bears its judgment in his body, walks out of the grave in victory, and pours out his Spirit to make them new. The grace that offends our pride is the only grace that can save us, because a forgiveness reserved for those who deserve it would leave every one of us condemned. But the mercy of Christ is not reserved for the deserving. It is given to the guilty, and everyone who truly receives it is never left as Christ found him.

The person Christ saves is not yet everything he will become, but neither is he what he once was. He has been placed upon a new road beneath a new Lord, and even his willingness to walk that road is the fruit of grace already at work within him. The Spirit who raised him from death will not abandon him halfway to glory. Day by day, through the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the fellowship and discipline of the church, and the ordinary obedience God himself supplies, Christ is forming his own likeness in those he purchased with his blood. Their steps will not be perfect in this life, but their destination is certain. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

Magun: Please pee in my mouth and save me
By Funke Egbemode

The news from Osun was bizarre, even by Nigerian standards.

A man was reportedly dying on the street. Those around him apparently believed he had encountered magun, an ancient Yoruba nightmare whose name roughly translates to “do not climb”. Magun is believed to be an instant killer, but this particular Osun instance had a solution.

The woman suspected to be the magun victim’s partner-in-sin should urinate in his mouth.

Ah.

There are deaths.

There are embarrassing deaths.

And then there are deaths where your alleged last hope is standing over you, saying, tragically,

“I don’t know this man.”

According to eyewitness accounts (in Yoruba) on social media, the woman refused. She reportedly denied being his lover. The desperate man begged. People around cursed and shouted.

The woman stood her ground.

“I don’t know him.”

My people, imagine climbing a fence with somebody and, when the DisCo cuts off the light while you’re still on top, your fellow climber suddenly says she has never seen you before.

This is why every business needs an exit strategy, especially illegal businesses.

Now, before somebody sends for the village herbalist to start a lecture on the origins of magun, let us establish something important. Magun belongs to Yoruba traditional belief and folklore. Researchers have documented beliefs in different varieties and supposed consequences, but that is not scientific proof that a charm caused any particular death. Sudden collapse during or after sex can have medical explanations, including cardiac arrest. That is why a woman cannot be accused of murder just because a man somersaults in her bed. Magun is not captured in our law books. Viewed from another angle, if your neighbour collapses, please call for medical help. Don’t form an emergency committee and start looking for urine.

That said, Yoruba folklore surrounding magun is enough to make a wandering husband reconsider his extracurricular timetable.

Because, according to tradition, magun does not come in one flavour.

There is reportedly má jè ìlà — don’t eat okro. Accounts of Yoruba traditional belief indeed identify an okro-associated form among the varieties.

Which means from today, ladies, when a perfectly healthy Yoruba man announces:

“I don’t eat okro.”

Don’t accuse him of anything.

Just look at him with side eyes, from head to toe. Then ask: “Since when?”

If he starts sweating before the soup arrives, I have said nothing.

Maybe he simply dislikes okro. Maybe.

There are also traditional accounts of varieties associated with water or particular prohibitions. The wider literature on magun stresses that its alleged forms, effects and antidotes vary considerably from practitioner to practitioner and community to community.

Our elders clearly believed that if a man insisted on inspecting another man’s compound, ordinary “no trespassing” signs were insufficient.

They allegedly installed spiritual CCTV.

Imagine living under a taboo that says don’t cross a river.

In Yorubaland?

Where will you go?

Your girlfriend says, “Darling, come to my village.”

You ask, “Any river?”

She says, “Just one small bridge.”

The relationship ends immediately.

“It’s not you, Bose. I need to work on myself.”

Work on yourself, really?

You are avoiding Osun River.

Then there is the one popularly described as the somersaulting magun.

This is the heavyweight champion of the belief.

Traditional accounts say the offending lover may somersault repeatedly—often described as three times—before dying.

Three!

Not one warning somersault so you can repent.

No VAR.

No appeal.

No Supreme Court.

According to the folklore, once the performance starts, the curtain closes.

And this is where my sympathy begins to develop a puncture.

Because why are you climbing another man’s fence in the first place?

Millions of unattached women walk around peacefully.

But no.

Some men see “married” and apparently read: Special offer.

Then there is the alleged urine remedy—the particularly humiliating version at the centre of this Osun story.

Imagine the negotiations.

“Please, save me!”

“Who? Do I know you?”

“Ah, Ajike”

“I don’t know him.”

“Moji, this is not a joke.”

Neighbours have gathered now.

Phones are recording.

Your ancestors are probably changing surnames.

And your supposed lover—the co-defendant in the matter—is insisting she has never met you since God created heaven and earth.

That is not merely heartbreak.

That is abandonment at the scene of the crime.

But beneath the laughter is something worth saying.

Adultery has always carried risks, with or without magun. Broken homes. Violence. Sexually transmitted infections. Public disgrace. Blackmail. Emotional wreckage. And, in some circumstances, medical emergencies.

You don’t need to believe in thunderbolts to understand consequences.

And you certainly should not watch a person convulsing, collapsing or struggling to breathe and conclude that what he needs is a bowl, a volunteer and fresh urine.

Get him medical help.

Let the doctors first deal with what science can establish.

If the family wants to discuss ancestors afterward, that meeting can hold when everybody is alive.

Still, Yoruba people knew how to name things.

Magun.

Don’t climb.

Two words.

No long sermon.

No PowerPoint presentation.

No marriage seminar.

Just:

Don’t. Climb.

Perhaps modern men require the updated version:

Dear Sir,

That fence you are admiring has an owner.

You do not know what is behind it.

You don’t know whether there is an angry husband, CCTV, disease, scandal, violence—or merely the spectacular humiliation of discovering at your hour of greatest need that your beloved co-conspirator has developed acute amnesia.

And if you are one of those gentlemen who mysteriously doesn’t eat okro, doesn’t drink gari, avoids rivers and becomes nervous whenever somebody mentions somersaulting…

My brother.

We are not accusing you.

We just want to know: exactly how many people’s fences have you been climbing?
